# P-A6: `--propose` fills entries class by class

**To:** the architect. **From:** the Ontology Template Team. **Date:** 2026-11-15.
**Status:** proposed. **Under:** decision 23, which accepted P-A6 as a template finding;
decision 29, which placed it in the backlog; decision 47, which put it next after v0.10.0;
and decision 49, which asked for this design: "the specific gap, proposed correction,
validation evidence, implementation boundaries, and architectural decisions required". §7
lists what is asked.

---

## 1. The gap

The BPO Testing Team's WP6 Phase A results, as reported:

> P-A6: `--propose` writes one reason, owner and review for every new finding of a check.
> A project that disposes by class (A5) cannot use it as it stands; we called
> `findings.propose()` once per class instead. A filter by rule, or by a list of
> identities, would do.

Read against the template at `79f915b`, it holds, and it has grown since it was reported:

- **No selection.** `tools/ontology/validate.py --propose` and `tools/ontology/iri_lint.py
  --propose` pass `verdict["new"]` to `findings.propose()`, which is every new finding of
  the check. `--reason`, `--owner` and `--review` are written into every proposed entry.
  `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` says so, and that it "is a decision about all of them". The only
  narrowing is the linter's file arguments, which select by file and nothing else.
- **The Python function already does it.** `findings.propose(records, ...)` takes any list
  of records. The team's workaround was to select the records themselves. So the gap is
  only on the command line: a project without its own script has no way to say "these
  findings, this reason".
- **Since v0.3.0 an entry has four more fields** (P-A7, decision 32): `validity`, `origin`,
  `resolution` and `classified_by`. `--propose` always writes them as `TODO` placeholders,
  which the register refuses. So even a project that proposes one class at a time edits
  four fields on every entry by hand. BPO's 3,749 entries in 17 classes would be about
  15,000 hand edits of values a person decided 17 times.

What a class is, in WP6: BPO's 17 classes were sorted by a tool of the port's own, and each
had one classification, owner and reason. Some follow a rule line ("every placement
finding"). Others don't: the 9 false alarms were APQC element names among one rule's
findings, and the 8 unsure ones were 8 terms with two different parents. A rule filter alone
cannot express those classes; a list of terms can.

## 2. The correction

**Selection, for both checks**, in `tools/findings.py` as one function, `select(records,
rules, wheres, focuses)`, which both CLIs call:

| Option | Selects the new findings whose | Repeatable |
|---|---|---|
| `--rule RULE` | shape or lint rule is one of these | yes |
| `--where WHERE` | shape set or file is one of these | yes |
| `--focus IRI` | term is one of these | yes |
| `--focus-file PATH` | term is listed in the file, one IRI per line, `#` comments and blank lines ignored | yes |

Values of one option are alternatives; different options must all hold. With no option, the
selection is every new finding, as now, so every existing invocation prints exactly what it
prints today.

**Nothing selected silently, nothing dropped silently:**
- stderr says how many were selected and how many new findings were left out: "12 of 340
  new finding(s) selected; 328 not selected, still new". The left-out ones stay new, and
  the gate still fails on them.
- A value that matches no new finding is refused with exit 2, naming the value, so that a
  mistyped rule doesn't print an empty proposal that looks like "nothing to do". A value that
  matches only findings already in the register is refused the same way, and the message
  says that they are already entered.
- `--focus-file` refuses a line that is not an absolute IRI.

**The classification, given by a person once per class** (§7, question 2, decides whether
this part is built). `--validity`, `--origin`, `--resolution`, `--classified-by` and
`--reference` would be written into each selected entry as given:
- **All or none.** If any of the four is given, all four must be given. A partial
  classification is refused, not completed with placeholders.
- **The register's own rules, before anything is printed.** The given values are checked by
  the function the register uses, `classification_problems`: `accepted` requires `real`,
  `reported` requires `--reference`, and so on, with the same messages. An inconsistent
  class is refused once, instead of producing 340 entries the register then refuses.
- **The person is named, never inferred.** `--classified-by` has no default: not git's user,
  not the owner. Its kind must be one of `config/review.yaml`'s, as in the register.
- **`origin: upstream`** requires each entry's own `upstream` field, which names the term,
  so it can't be given once for a class. It is refused on the command line, and such
  entries are classified by hand, as now.
- **Without the flags,** the placeholders are written as now.

## 3. Validation evidence

On planted findings, in `tests/test_findings.py`, through both CLIs:
- each option selects what it says and nothing else;
- two options together narrow the selection, and one option repeated widens it;
- no option prints today's output, byte for byte;
- the stderr counts add up to the new findings;
- a value matching nothing, or only entered findings, exits 2 and names the value;
- a malformed focus file is refused;
- the selected entries, pasted with their values filled in, are accepted by the register and
  leave exactly the others new;
- class by class over a planted partition, the gate passes at the end, and no finding is
  entered twice.

If question 2 is approved:
- a partial classification is refused;
- every inconsistent combination the register refuses is refused here, with the same
  message;
- `--classified-by` with an unknown kind is refused;
- `origin: upstream` is refused;
- without the flags, the placeholders are still written, and the register still refuses
  them.

Then mutation tests on the selection, the counts, the refusals and the CLI wiring, as for
P-A5.

No BPO measurement is proposed. The gap is the command line, not scale: `judge` and
`propose` already run at BPO's 3,749 entries (WP6 Phase A), and selection is one pass over
the new findings. BPO's actual classes are in the port's private records, which this work
does not read.

## 4. Boundaries

What it changes: `tools/findings.py` (`select`, and the classification check reused, not
copied), the `--propose` options of `validate.py` and `iri_lint.py`, `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md`'s
register section, and the tests. These are owned files, so a project takes them by the P-A2
upgrade.

What it does not change:
- what a check finds;
- a finding's identity or digest;
- `judge`, the gate or decision 11's policy;
- the register's format, fields or classification rules (decision 32);
- `findings.py --classify`;
- the order or text of entries `--propose` writes for a given selection.

Not included, though nearby:
- **`tools/review.py --propose` and `tools/ontology/candidates.py --propose`.** They propose
  entries for a different register, the review of detection candidates (item 12), and
  nothing reported a gap there.
- **Reclassifying existing entries in bulk.** `--propose` is for new findings; a register
  already filled is edited as now.
- **Selection by message text or pattern.** It would make a class depend on the wording of
  a message, which the digest already pins.
- **No WP6 finding or decision is reopened.** In particular, decision 32's classification
  stays as it is.

## 5. Compatibility

Every option is new and optional, and nothing is renamed or removed. A script calling
`findings.propose()` directly, as BPO's did, is unaffected. A project upgraded by the P-A2
procedure takes the three tools and the guide.

## 6. Decision 32

Decision 32: "No tool should populate `real`, `false-alarm`, or `unsure` automatically. The
decision to classify a finding must come from an identified reviewer. A migration tool may
prepare entries for review but must not impersonate human judgment."

Here, no value is chosen by the tool. A person types the classification and their own name
once, and the tool copies them into the entries that person selected, as `--reason` is
copied now. Whether a class-level judgement is consistent with decision 32 is for the
architect to say, not for this design to assume. That is why §2's classification part is a
separate question. Without it, P-A6 still closes the reported gap (selection), and the
classification stays hand-written per entry.

## 7. What we ask

1. **Selection.** Proposed: `--rule`, `--where`, `--focus` and `--focus-file` on both
   checks' `--propose`, with the counts and refusals of §2. Or: `--rule` only, as the team
   first suggested, though it can't express classes like WP6's 9 false alarms.
2. **The classification on the command line.** Proposed: all four fields given once per
   selection by a named person, checked by the register's rules, `origin: upstream`
   excluded (§2, §6). Or: not built; placeholders as now.
3. **Exact identities.** Proposed: not built; a term list selects every finding about those
   terms. Or: also `--select FILE`, entries in the register's own format, for a class that
   splits one term's findings.
4. **Release.** Proposed: P-A6 alone as v0.11.0, under `RELEASING.md`. Then P-A8, then
   P-A4, each designed before it is built.

Size: smaller than P-A5. One function and four options shared by two tools, a check reused,
a section of the guide, and the tests. Nothing is built until it is approved.
